title: CSP, Proxies & Reverse Proxies
objectives: Write a Content-Security-Policy that blocks XSS without breaking the app
Explain what forward and reverse proxies each control in the request path
Handle X-Forwarded-* headers and compression at the correct layer
body:
# CSP, Proxies & Reverse Proxies

## The problem
An XSS bug in one template can dump every user's data. Patching each input is never enough; you want a policy the browser enforces even when your code fails. Meanwhile, in production your app almost never talks to the internet directly: a reverse proxy terminates TLS, compresses, caches, and routes. Both layers quietly rewrite what your app said, so you must understand what each one controls.

## Content-Security-Policy
CSP is a response header declaring which sources of script, style, image, and connection the page may use:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com; frame-ancestors 'none'
```

- `default-src` is the fallback for any directive you do not spell out.
- `script-src 'unsafe-inline'` largely disables XSS protection - avoid it.
- Nonces (`script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m'`) allow specific inline scripts safely.
- `report-uri` / `report-to` stream violations to your monitoring.
- `frame-ancestors 'none'` blocks clickjacking framing (replaces X-Frame-Options).

## Forward vs reverse proxy
- Forward proxy: sits in front of clients (corporate egress, filtering, caching).
- Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers (nginx, Envoy, cloud load balancers).

A reverse proxy typically owns:
- TLS termination and HTTP/2 for many backends.
- Routing `/api` to service A and `/` to static assets.
- Compression, rate limiting, IP allowlists.
- Adding `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` - which your app must trust only from the proxy, or clients will spoof their own IP.

## The classic proxy bugs
- The app builds absolute `http://` URLs because it cannot see the original scheme -> honor `X-Forwarded-Proto`.
- Compression plus attacker-reflected content plus secrets in one response enables BREACH-style attacks; do not compress responses where secrets sit next to reflected input.
- Double compression: the app gzips and the proxy gzips again, breaking some clients.

## Decision framework
- Serving user-facing HTML? -> CSP with nonces, rolled out as Report-Only first.
- Multiple services behind one domain? -> reverse proxy path routing keeps cookies and CORS simple.
- Terminate TLS at the edge or in the app? -> edge for public traffic; internal mTLS when compliance demands end-to-end encryption.

## Best practices
- Roll out CSP in Report-Only mode and watch violation reports before enforcing.
- Terminate TLS once at the proxy and redirect http -> https there.
- Configure trust for X-Forwarded-* so your app reads client IPs correctly and only from the proxy.
- Keep compression decisions in one layer, not two.

## Common mistakes
- Adding `'unsafe-inline'` to make the console quiet without investigating why.
- Assuming headers survive every hop: hop-by-hop headers are consumed by proxies.
- Trusting `X-Forwarded-For` from any source, letting clients spoof IPs.
- Serving static assets and the API on one domain but scoping cookie `Path` wrong, leaking session cookies to static handlers.

exercise.prompt: Implement hasUnsafeInlineScript(policy): given a CSP header value split by semicolons, find the script-src directive and return true when it contains 'unsafe-inline'. Report the finding in the preview output.
hints: Split the policy on ; and trim each directive before matching.
Find the directive that starts with script-src, not default-src.
The starter always reports ok - that is the bug: it never inspects the policy.

questions.prompt: Which CSP change allows specific inline scripts without 'unsafe-inline'?
questions.explanation: A nonce generated per response lets the browser run only the inline scripts you tagged, keeping everything else blocked.

options: From any client that sends the header
Only from your own reverse proxy
questions.explanation: Anyone can send X-Forwarded-For directly to your app; only values set by your own trusted proxy are meaningful.

questions.prompt: Why deploy CSP in Report-Only mode first?
options: To collect violation reports and fix breakage before enforcing
Nonces only work in Report-Only mode
questions.explanation: Report-Only records what would be blocked, so you can tune the policy before enforcement breaks real pages.
